content.text: Deleting a secret in a new commit, or moving it to a
.env

file, only changes the latest version of your code. Every earlier commit, every clone and every fork still holds the key, and the key still works. Revoke and rotate it first; rewriting Git history is a cleanup step that's often unnecessary once the old key is dead.
A developer on a small team opens a pull request on the company's public storefront plugin. A reviewer spots the payment provider's API key in
appsettings.json
. The developer empties the value, moves the key to a
.env
file listed in
.gitignore

, and pushes a commit called "Move API key to .env". The review passes, the branch is merged, and nobody touches the key itself. A month later the provider's dashboard shows refunds that nobody on the team issued. The key was still in the first commit, and it still worked.
The common misconception
The belief: once a secret is gone from the code, by a new commit or by moving it to an env file, it's safe again.
Every tool you look at agrees. The file on GitHub shows an empty value.
git grep

finds nothing. Code search finds nothing. Moving secrets out of source files is also genuinely good advice, so the commit looks like the responsible fix. But all of those tools show the latest version of the code, and a leaked secret doesn't care about the latest version. It cares about every copy that already exists, and about whether the key is still valid.
What actually happens
A commit keeps the old version forever
A
commit

is a snapshot of the whole project. Deleting a line adds a new snapshot; it doesn't edit the old ones. We reproduced the story in a scratch repository on Git 2.54, with an obviously fake key, and searched for it after the "fix":

Notice the last line. The cleanup commit itself shows the key, as the line it removed. Anyone who reads the pull request diff or the commit page sees it, and a fresh clone of the repository returned the same two commits.
Copies don't receive your cleanup

Even a full history rewrite only changes the repository you push it to. GitHub's guide on removing sensitive data lists where the commits "may still be accessible elsewhere": "In any clones or forks of your repository", "Directly via their SHA-1 hashes in cached views on GitHub" and "Through any pull requests that reference them". It's blunt about the first: "You cannot remove sensitive data from other users' clones of your repository." CI caches, build logs and laptops are copies too.

A rewrite can even help an attacker. GitHub warns that "clueful users with an existing clone will notice the history divergence and can use it to quickly and easily find the sensitive data still in their clone that you removed from the central repository."
An env file moves the key, it doesn't change it
The value in
.env

is the same string that sits in history, so the move changes where your next deploy reads it, not whether the leaked copy works. Env files and variables have their own exposure, too: OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet notes that environment variables "are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps." And if the key ships inside a mobile app, it's public whatever you do in Git, as the article "Your Mobile App Can't Keep a Secret" explains.
Only revocation makes the leaked copy useless
An API key is a
bearer credential

: whoever presents it gets in. So the fix happens at the provider, not in the repository. GitHub's guide starts there: "as a first step you need to revoke and/or rotate that secret. Once the secret is revoked or rotated, it can no longer be used for access, and that may be sufficient to solve your problem." Its secret scanning docs add that removing secrets from history "is time-intensive and often unnecessary if you've already revoked the credential." OWASP's incident response order is revocation,
rotation
, deletion from the exposed system, then logging: "Who had access? When did they use it?"
Closing the leak in the right order

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Empty the value, move the key to .env, push. Incident closed?
git commit -am "Move API key to .env"
git push
# The key is still in the previous commit, in this commit's diff,
# in every clone and fork, and it still works at the provider.

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# 1. Revoke the key in the provider's console, issue a new one,
#    and store the new key in your secret store or CI secrets.
# 2. Keep local env files out of Git for good
echo '.env' >> .gitignore
git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch .env
# 3. List every commit that ever contained the old key
git log --all --oneline -S 'FAKE-KEY-0000-DO-NOT-USE'
# 4. Only if history must be cleaned: rewrite a fresh clone
git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal --replace-text ../leaked.txt
git push --force --mirror origin

content.text: Step 1 is the only one that stops the leaked key from working, and it's the one the wrong tab skips. Steps 2 and 3 cost minutes. Step 4 uses the commands from GitHub's guide;
--sensitive-data-removal
needs git-filter-repo 2.47 or later. Git's own documentation calls the older
git filter-branch
a tool whose "use is not recommended" and points to git filter-repo instead.

rows.text: A new commit that deletes the key
On the server only; clones and forks keep it

content.text: A history rewrite takes coordination and can take days, and the key works the whole time. Revoke it first, then decide whether a rewrite is still worth it. GitHub Support only helps remove cached data "in cases where we determine that the risk can't be mitigated by rotating affected credentials."

blocks.title: A rewrite has real side effects

content.text: GitHub lists them: commit hashes change "and all commits that came after", branch protections that block force pushes "will have to be turned off (at least temporarily)", closed pull requests lose their diffs, and signatures are removed. And if a teammate with an old clone "simply runs git pull followed by git push, the sensitive data will return."

blocks.title: Let GitHub block the next one

content.text: Push protection "blocks pushes that contain secrets before they reach your repository." For your own account it's on by default and stops you pushing secrets to public repositories; for a repository it must be enabled, and needs GitHub Secret Protection. Secret scanning runs free on public repositories and scans "your entire Git history on all branches".
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Write the runbook before you need it

content.text: For each secret, note who can revoke it, how to issue a new one and where the app reads it. OWASP's cheat sheet asks for exactly this, including "Who is the point of contact during an incident".
When a secret leaks, revoke it at the provider, issue a new one, put it in your secret store and redeploy. Moving the old value somewhere else doesn't count.

items.title: Check how the old key was used

content.text: Read the provider's access logs for the exposure window. Look for calls from unknown addresses or actions your app never makes.

items.title: Decide whether history still needs cleaning

content.text: Rotation usually ends the risk. Rewrite with git-filter-repo only when the data can't be rotated, such as personal data, and plan for clones, forks and open pull requests.

items.title: Stop the next leak at the source

content.text: Ignore env files, turn on push protection and secret scanning, and add a pre-commit secret scan, which OWASP suggests so secrets are caught "before commit/PR".
Key takeaways

items.text: Deleting a secret in a new commit leaves it in every earlier commit, and the cleanup diff shows it too.
Clones, forks, caches and pull requests keep their copies; a history rewrite can't reach them.
file changes where it's stored, not whether the leaked copy works.
Revoke and rotate first: it's the only step that makes the leaked key useless.
Treat history rewriting as optional cleanup, and use push protection to stop the next leak.
